title: Uncanny host Danny Robins: 'I love the idea of ghosts existing'
excerpt: Though Danny Robins is the UK's undisputed king of the paranormal, he's still never seen a ghost – but he's keeping an open mind.
content:
Culture

Uncanny host Danny Robins: ‘I love the idea of ghosts existing. I really want it to be real'

Billed as the biggest ever crowd-sourced investigation into the supernatural, Uncanny has covered dozens of real-life stories

22 Nov 2026

Share

“If you imagine being Santa Claus at Christmas, that’s basically what my Halloween is like.” It’s three days before the spookiest night of the year, and Big Issue is catching up with the UK’s undisputed king of the paranormal, Danny Robins. 

It’s almost a decade since Danny (then primarily a comedy writer) created his first supernatural podcast, Haunted… but it was in 2021 when things that go bump in the night took over his life. That year, he created The Battersea Poltergeist podcast, which opened the (suitably creaking) door for Uncanny.

Billed as the biggest ever crowd-sourced investigation into the supernatural, Uncanny has covered dozens of real-life stories. Danny is the even-handed host, flanked by a champion of Team Believer on the one side, a representative for Team Sceptic on the other. It has spawned a community who keep the conversation going through social media, online forums and theatres all over the country. BBC Two snapped the show up for telly. And next year, Danny will embark on the first Uncanny arena tour across the UK and Ireland. 

Beyond all the incarnations of Uncanny, his award-winning spooky play 2:22 A Ghost Story has also been a huge hit all over the UK and has just opened in New York. This week, the Danny-verse takes another leap forward as his TV drama The Witch Farm comes to BBC One. Following a young family as they move to rural Wales and are caught up in a chilling series of unexplained events, the story is based on the real experiences of Liz Rich and her husband Bill. 

Danny previously examined the case in a terrifyingly popular podcast, but he hopes to reach yet another new audience this time – “the kind of people who enjoy a Line of Duty or a Broadchurch”. With unexplained noises, alarming apparitions, mysterious animal deaths, rumours of satanic rituals, and (maybe scariest of all) a runaway energy meter that costs the family a fortune – it’s strong fare for a Sunday night.

You must have heard more paranormal stories than almost anyone. What was it about the Witch Farm story that made it stand out? 

It’s that thing that has hit me at a few points in my career: when you talk to somebody and you get this very visceral sense that they are still frightened. That’s what I got when I spoke to Liz. And when you watch how the sequence of events unfolded, it really is like a horror movie come to life. 

It’s really clear how much of an impact these events had on Liz and her family. How do you make sure you’re looking after the real people at the core of these stories? 

I’m really glad to say that everyone who’s been on Uncanny has had a positive experience out of it. We stay in touch with the vast majority of people. With Liz specifically, on The Witch Farm, we talk regularly. For her, telling this story has been an incredibly positive, therapeutic thing. When you go through those things, you need to talk about them. You need to somehow make sense of this fear. You want to feel vindicated and validated.

Do you think that ghost sightings perhaps go up when mental health support is cut?

I certainly couldn’t give a definite answer on that, but I know anecdotally that reports of paranormal experience went up a lot during Covid, which is revealing. That was a period when we were haunted by our houses – these previously cosy places became quite claustrophobic and oppressive. 

You can look at the booms in paranormal interest post First World War, post Second World War – right back to the Jacobean period, the era of witch hunting and plague and religious division. All these periods when our society is fractured and frightened and uncertain, when our mental health is put to the test, you definitely see booms of paranormal interest. Is that us wanting to find magic in a bleak world? Is it us wanting to try and find answers when there is uncertainty? Or is it literally paranormal activity manifesting? 

Has your opinion changed since Uncanny started? Have you become more Team Believer or more Team Sceptic? 

Without wanting to sound like a contestant on The X Factor, I feel like I’ve been on a journey. If you listen to me making the very first show I ever did, you hear a more sceptic me. But you can’t be exposed to all of these stories and not have it eat away at your resolve a little bit. 

I am someone who loves the idea of ghosts existing. I think the idea that death is not the end is a wonderful idea. And I just love the idea of magic. I do really love the idea that we haven’t discovered everything about our universe and that there’s something more out there, just waiting in the shadows for us. So I really want it to be real, but I haven’t had that experience that pushes me over the edge.

Not for want of trying, right? 

I know! Come on, ghosts! 

If anyone is going to see a ghost, it seems only fair you should. You’ve done so much for them.

Well, they’re not keeping their end of the bargain. But I do enjoy existing in a state of uncertainty, and I think there’s a lot to be said for being somewhere in the middle. Uncanny would be a very different show if I took a really strong position and pushed an agenda, whether it was belief or scepticism. 

I enjoy being torn and listening with an open mind. It’s something that is in short supply in our world. One of the big messages of Uncanny and all of the things I do is: keep an open mind, listen to people and don’t dismiss things too quickly.

The first two episodes of The Witch Farm are on BBC iPlayer from 22 November; the series begins at 9pm that night on BBC One. Uncanny is on BBC Sounds
